assessments.reason: A single global score is the highest-value manipulation target in the system: ballot stuffing and self-promotion concentrate on it, and the note's comparison rejects this option outright. The design's controls (no self-rating weight, evidence-ID dedup, per-identity caps) exist precisely to deny a global number this leverage.

A global rating that allegations can move is a smear weapon: the design requires claims to remain allegations, a signed equal-auth right of reply, and no unilateral score change, none of which a single global verdict preserves.

A global score does not itself bound flooding; the design's bounds are local controls (claim rate limits, evidence byte caps, operator-chosen moderation caps). A central score adds an adjudication bottleneck without adding a bound.

Sybil identity cost is unresolved and open federation cannot guarantee identity continuity; a global score maximizes the payoff for both Sybil farming and whitewashing a burned identity into a fresh global rating.
Colluding evidence producers can still deceive, and there is no global oracle to appeal to; a global score gives successful collusion global effect instead of containing it to one local view.

A scalar collapses provenance: transparency-log inclusion (RFC 9162) and COSE receipts (RFC 9942) prove that a statement was published / included at issuance, not that the claim is true or attributable to a named party without key binding. A global number discards exactly the distinction the evidence layer exists to keep.

This is the design's stated control set: no self-rating weight, evidence IDs deduplicated, per-identity contribution capped, and allegations never rewarded. GossipSub v1.1 is the working precedent that locally computed, unshared scores with thresholds can drive local decisions without becoming a portable global truth.

Claims are allegations, not verdicts; claim and reply carry equal authentication, rate, and size rules, and the subject receives an equivalent reply opportunity. The design's deterministic thresholds act only on attributable evidence classes, never on unverified public claims, which have no direct verdict weight.

The design bounds claims directly: 3 claims per claimant/subject/day and 64 KiB of evidence references per claim, with moderation and privacy-redacted commitments; operators choose caps for their own view.

Local identity-continuity evidence and careful decay mitigate whitewashing (GossipSub likewise retains scores across disconnects so a peer cannot reset by reconnecting), but Sybil identity cost is unresolved and open federation cannot guarantee identity continuity. The criterion is honestly bounded, not met; whether the residual risk is acceptable depends on the demonstrated-need review.

Independently verifiable scoped evidence and local weighting contain collusion to the views that accepted the evidence, and no collusion-proof claim is made; but colluding evidence producers can still deceive a local view, and no measurement or deployment evidence yet shows how much. Recorded unknown rather than asserted.

Auto-reputation evidence classes are explicit and attributable (protocol violations, scoped receipt contradiction, availability timeout, successful valid service). An invalid signature does not authenticate its purported signer: a bad-signature event counts against a supplying peer only with authenticated session/peer binding plus signed evidence, otherwise it is retained unattributed with no rating penalty. Log inclusion and COSE receipts supply the publication proofs, and inclusion proves publication only.
With no automated rating there is no score to stuff, farm, or game; allegations cannot reward the allegant because nothing computes a verdict from them.
No rating exists for a smear to move. Claims and replies remain signed log events under equal rules, and any consequence is a human review decision, not a unilateral automated change.

The claims log's own bounds (claim rate limits and evidence byte caps) apply whether or not ratings are computed, so flooding is bounded even in the conservative mode; what is given up is automated reaction, not the caps.

Adopting none creates no rating surface for Sybils to exploit and no score to whitewash into; the unresolved Sybil identity cost stays an explicit known-unknown for any future automation instead of being silently inherited.
Collusion has no automated verdict to capture; coordinated claims remain allegations in an auditable log, subject to human review with the evidence and its provenance intact.

The append-only signed claims log and its inclusion proofs are retained unchanged; attribution discipline (including never attributing an invalid signature to its claimed signer) is a property of the log and evidence rules, not of the rating automation this option omits.

criteria.question: Does the option resist manipulation and self-promotion (no self-rating weight, deduplicated evidence, per-identity caps, allegations never rewarded)?
Does the option keep claims as allegations rather than verdicts, with an equal-authentication right of reply and no unilateral score change?
Does the option bound spam and flooding (claim rate and byte caps, moderation with privacy-redacted commitments)?
Does the option resist Sybil and whitewashing attacks, honestly bounding what open federation cannot guarantee about identity continuity?
Does the option bound collusion (independently verifiable scoped evidence, local weighting), without claiming a global oracle?

Does the option keep evidence verifiable and correctly attributed (signed commitments and inclusion proofs prove publication, not truth; an invalid signature is never attributed to its claimed signer)?

decision.reason: A global scalar reputation authority is rejected: it maximizes manipulation, retaliation, Sybil, and collusion payoff while collapsing the provenance that inclusion proofs exist to preserve. Local evidence-weighted policy is the design's default candidate (explicit attributable evidence classes, deterministic local thresholds, equal-auth reply, claim caps), but two of its criteria (Sybil/whitewashing, collusion) are honestly unknown today, and implementation/adoption is contingent on a demonstrated abuse/workload need or the versioned-design evidence threshold (S1.88-S1.91, S1.99). No-automated-rating remains a valid conservative deployment mode in the meantime. Standing conclusion, unchanged: no public allegation alone changes a rating, and no collusion-proof claim is made.

experiments.method: Before any automated local rating is enabled, review observed abuse signals (claim volume and rate-limit pressure, attributable protocol violations, spam/flooding pressure, Sybil/whitewashing attempts) against the design's proposed starting thresholds and record whether a demonstrated need exists. Planned only in this slice; no deployment exists and no abuse data was observed, so no need is asserted and no measurements are claimed.

limitations: The validator checks structural completeness and traceability only, not factual truth; this artifact is a synthesis of the B26 source ledger (evidence checked 2026-11-12) plus a fresh primary-source re-read of the three cited references on 2026-11-14, which confirmed the cited claims (GossipSub scores are locally computed and not shared; RFC 9162 logs prove inclusion/publication, not claim truth, and a log can present inconsistent views; RFC 9942 receipts prove VDS properties at issuance).

No deployment or abuse data exists for this design: the demonstrated-need review is unmeasured by design (contingent tier), so the Sybil/whitewashing and collusion criteria for the local-policy option are unknown rather than estimated.

The design's numeric thresholds (3 claims per claimant/subject/day, 64 KiB evidence references, quarantine and priority-band counts) are proposed starting defaults recorded in the versioned design, not externally verified or universal weights; this artifact does not endorse them as tuned values.
The GossipSub specification is a living document (v1.1 revision r8, 2021-12-14, at access time); its scoring is precedent for local thresholds, not evidence of globally fair or portable reputation.
No reputation code was written or run in this slice; findings rest on the cited specifications, the repo research note, and the versioned design record.

options.label: Adopt a global scalar reputation authority
Defer to demonstrated need: local evidence-weighted reputation policy (design default candidate)
Adopt none: no automated rating until review (signed claims log and human review only)

question: Against the abuse-protection criteria for #9147 (statements S1.88, S1.89, S1.90, S1.91, S1.99), should ID/Atlas adopt a global scalar reputation authority, adopt local evidence-weighted reputation policy when a demonstrated need triggers it, or adopt no automated rating?

source_ledger.undated_reason: Living libp2p specification (v1.1, latest revision r8 dated 2021-12-14 in its status table). Re-read fresh on 2026-11-14 for this result: each peer's score is locally computed from observed behaviour and is not shared; thresholds prune, de-gossip, de-publish, and graylist at descending scores; scores are retained for a period after disconnect so peers cannot easily reset a negative score by reconnecting; application-specific scoring is pluggable; structural quotas and adaptive gossip, not scores alone, carry the Sybil/eclipse resistance.

RFC 9162, Certificate Transparency Version 2.0 (Experimental, December 2021). Re-read fresh on 2026-11-14: logs are append-only Merkle trees; a signed timestamp and later inclusion proof evidence that an entry was submitted and included; logs detect misissuance rather than preventing it, and the document itself notes a misbehaving log can present inconsistent views to different clients. Inclusion therefore proves publication, not the truth of what was logged.

RFC 9942, CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts (Standards Track, June 2026). Re-read fresh on 2026-11-14: COSE Receipts are signed proofs of properties of a Verifiable Data Structure that are true when the receipt was issued - proof of inclusion, consistency, disclosure, or non-inclusion - with concrete encodings for the RFC 9162 Merkle structures. A receipt proves the VDS state it attests, not the truth of the underlying claim.

Repo research note for slice B26; its header records evidence checked 2026-11-12 and scope reputation-abuse. It tabulates the five abuse classes with the design's default controls and residual limitations, compares the three options (global scalar rejected; local evidence-weighted default; no automated rating a valid conservative mode), and states the conclusion this artifact formalizes.

Repo versioned design record for the ID/Atlas summit, Part B, sections 'Routing validation and reputation policy' and 'Public claims log privacy/fairness' (statements S1.88-S1.91, S1.99). It defines the explicit auto-reputation evidence classes, the bad-signature attribution rule, the proposed deterministic thresholds and claim caps, equal claim/reply rules, and that inclusion proves publication only.
